newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges S.Africa to resist China pressure.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges S.Africa to resist China pressure.

text.p: Taipei urged Pretoria on Friday to live up to its vow to maintain high-level contacts with Taiwan after switching ties to rival China, saying South Africa should resist "barbaric demands" from Beijing.
A Taipei newspaper said on Friday that Beijing was demanding that South Africa sharply downgrade its ties with Taiwan after Beijing and Pretoria normalise relations sometime in 1997.
Taiwan's foreign ministry, trying to limit damage from the defection of its biggest diplomatic partner, issued a statement urging Pretoria to stand by its pledge of high-level ties.

"South African President Mandela has repeatedly promised us that both sides will maintain 'the highest level relations short of full diplomatic recognition' after Taiwan and South Africa adjust their ties," a ministry statement said.
"We have not heard of any change in this position. We hope Pretoria can stick to its position and not succumb to communist China's unreasonable, barbaric demand," the ministry said.
President Nelson Mandela said in November that Pretoria would cut diplomatic ties with Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and recognise the island's communist rival by the end of 1997.
The United Daily News said Beijing had drafted a Sino-South African joint communique in which South Africa would recognise Taiwan as an inalienable part of China.
The communique would be the mechanism by which Beijing and Pretoria established diplomatic relations, it said.
The newspaper said the word "recognise" was much stronger in diplomatic terms than the formulations accepted by most western powers in their joint communiques with China.

The United States, Britain and Australia all "acknowledge" that Taiwan is part of China, while Italy and Canada merely "take note of" this, it said. Japan uses the phrase "understand and respect" while Germany makes no mention of Taiwan at all.
The foreign ministry said South Africa should live up to its promises to avoid further damaging ties with Taiwan.
"We are not a bit surprised by communist China's barbaric attitude," the statement said. "South Africa should maintain its independence and not to be intimidated by communist China."
Beijing said on Thursday that bilateral talks to establish Sino-South African ties were on track.

South Africa is the largest of only 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in central America and Africa -- that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government rather than the communist mainland's People's Republic.

Beijing, Taipei's rival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards Taiwan as a rebel province ineligible for foreign ties and has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.
